title: Finland’s Gutsy Pictures Pacts With MTV, Germany’s Zeitsprung, Sweden’s Götafilm on Zaida Bergroth’s ‘Dangerous Woman’ (EXCLUSIVE)
description: Value-driven Finnish outfit Gutsy Pictures headed by Marika Makaroff (“Moominvalley,” “L/Over”) has secured a greenlight from MTV Finland and added
body:
Value-driven Finnish outfit Gutsy Pictures headed by Marika Makaroff (“Moominvalley,” “L/Over”) has secured a greenlight from MTV Finland and added co-producers Zeitsprung in Germany and Götafilm in Sweden for the psycho-thriller “Dangerous Woman.”Already pre-bought by TV4 in Sweden, the six-parter created by Makaroff will be directed by the established Zaida Bergroth, credited for the crowd-pleaser and Finnish Oscar entry “Tove.” Joining the key creatives are BAFTA-winner Kevin Rundle (“Gangs of London,” “The Thaw,” “Eastenders”), who reunites with Gutsy after their successful collaboration on the Canneseries selected “L/Over,” one of MTV’s biggest hits earlier this year.


	The story centers on Laura, a middle-aged woman at the peak of her career, caught violently attacking a male visitor at an interior design fair. Once arrested, bigger secrets begin to surface. The woman who’s been hiding under a different identity for years, is also linked to an unsolved murder case. As the story of her life unwraps across three timelines, we start to question if it’s her where  the real danger lies.
	

	“I’ve wanted to tell this story for 10 years, but when I first wrote it, the idea felt almost too extreme,” Makaroff said, before adding: “Today, hatred has become increasingly normalized, and I wanted to explore what happens when it moves beyond words and becomes physical.”

	Makaroff, who opened up about her own experience of abuse while promoting “L/Over” in 2025, said she’s approached the character of Laura in “Dangerous Woman” “with compassion”. “She [Laura] has spent a lifetime being belittled, dominated and abused, and eventually reaches her breaking point. Through her, I’m asking a difficult question: can violence or revenge ever be justified? And if we become those we hate, who does that serve?”

	“The series is a mix of dark humor, psychological thriller and social drama, but ultimately it is a story about humanity, grace and forgiveness,” she observed.
	

	Added Janne Vakio, commissions and content development manager at MTV, “At MTV, we believe great stories become even stronger through great partnerships. ‘Dangerous Woman’ brings together a bold creative vision, top-tier talent and producers from three markets with a shared ambition: to create a distinctive Nordic drama that can resonate both at home and internationally.”

	The series is due to go into production later this year.“Dangerous Woman” is one of 11 international premium dramas selected for the co-production pitch showcase Mind the Gap, hosted by Serielizados Pro (Oct 21-24), the industry sidebar of Barcelona’s series festival Serielizados.

schema.headline: Finland’s Gutsy Pictures Pacts With MTV, Germany’s Zeitsprung, Sweden’s Götafilm on Zaida Bergroth’s ‘Dangerous Woman’ (EXCLUSIVE)

title: Kore-eda Hirokazu to Receive Cinema Honorary Award From Singapore Film Festival, Yim Soon-rye to Head Asian Competition Jury
description: The Singapore International Film Festival (SGIFF) will honor Japanese filmmaker Kore-eda Hirokazu with its Cinema Honorary Award and has named Korea
body:
The Singapore International Film Festival (SGIFF) will honor Japanese filmmaker Kore-eda Hirokazu with its Cinema Honorary Award and has named Korean director Yim Soon-rye jury head of its Asian Feature Film Competition. 

	The 37th edition of SGIFF runs Oct. 21 to Nov. 1.

	Kore-eda will attend a special presentation of “Look Back” on Oct. 24, marking the film’s Southeast Asia premiere ahead of its Oct. 29 theatrical release. He will also join an In Conversation With dialogue session that day, where he will be presented with the honorary award, the festival’s top prize for filmmakers who have made a lasting mark on Asian cinema.
	

	Kore-eda has built his career on intimate dramas centered on the family unit, tracing the friction between individuals and the social structures around them. His 2018 film “Shoplifters” won the Palme d’Or at the Cannes Film Festival, the first Japanese film to take the top prize in more than two decades. His subsequent films “Broker” and “Monster” drew both commercial and critical success, cementing his standing as one of Japan’s most prominent directors. Earlier credits include “Nobody Knows” and “Like Father, Like Son.”


	“Look Back” marks the first live-action feature adaptation of any manga by Fujimoto Tatsuki. The film follows Fujino, an elementary school student whose confidence as her class’s star cartoonist is upended when a reclusive classmate, Kyomoto, proves to be a far superior artist. Their rivalry curdles into obsession, and even after the two eventually connect and forge a friendship through their shared pursuit of manga, an opportunity to create a serial later arrives and pulls them apart. The film competed for the Golden Lion at the Venice Film Festival.
	

	Yim, who studied filmmaking at the University of Paris 8, debuted with “Three Friends” in 1996 and went on to direct “Waikiki Brothers,” the box office hit “Forever the Moment,” “The Whistleblower,” “Little Forest” and “The Point Men.” She has also spent 12 years as president of an animal rights association and co-leads the Korean Center for Gender Equality in Film. Yim will speak at SGIFF Industry Days on Oct. 27.

	SGIFF’s industry arm, SGIFF Pro, is expanding this year, with Industry Days growing from three to four days. Programming will include talks from cinematographer Ashizawa Akiko, laureate of the 2026 Pierre Angénieux Tribute awarded at the Cannes Film Festival earlier this year, and filmmaker Fukada Koji, whose Singapore co-production “Nagi Notes” will screen in the festival’s Horizon section.

	New additions to SGIFF Pro this year include Off Campus, a four-day field trip pairing film school students with industry professionals; the Pitching Forum, aimed at connecting international projects with decision-makers and local co-production partners to position Singapore as a regional hub; and Parallax, a free interdisciplinary sidebar examining the intersection of filmmaking, AI and immersive technology, with participants from Amazon MGM Studios, SM Entertainment, Adobe, Largo.ai and Ubac Studio.

	Founded in 1987, SGIFF is organized by Singapore International Film Festival Ltd., a nonprofit supported by the Infocomm Media Development Authority. SGIFF Pro comprises five programs in total: the Industry Days conference, the Asian Producers Network, the Pitching Forum, Off Campus and Parallax.

schema.headline: Kore-eda Hirokazu to Receive Cinema Honorary Award From Singapore Film Festival, Yim Soon-rye to Head Asian Competition Jury

title: ‘Practical Magic 2’ Casts a Spell Over U.K., Ireland Box Office as Oasis Doc Rocks No. 2
description: Warner Bros.’ “Practical Magic 2” cast a winning spell over the U.K. and Ireland box office, dethroning “Spider-Man: Brand New Day” after a six-week
body:
Warner Bros.’ “Practical Magic 2” cast a winning spell over the U.K. and Ireland box office, dethroning “Spider-Man: Brand New Day” after a six-week reign to claim the top spot with an opening weekend of £2.7 million ($3.7 million).

	Disney followed closely in second position with the cinema rollout of “Oasis: Don’t Look Back in Anger,” which captured $3.5 million across its debut frame. 20th Century Fox’s thriller “Pressure” rounded out the new release trio at the summit, taking third place with $2.7 million.
	

	Universal’s “The Odyssey” held firm in fourth place during its ninth week on release, collecting $1.2 million. The tentpole pushed its cume to $114.3 million. 


	Sony’s superhero juggernaut “Spider-Man: Brand New Day” moved to fifth position in its seventh frame, generating $1.1 ,illion. The blockbuster’s running total reached $132.7 million, overtaking “Spider-Man: No Way Home,” “Avatar,” and “No Time to Die” to claim the No. 3 spot on the all-time U.K. and Ireland box office chart, trailing only “Star Wars: The Force Awakens” and “Skyfall.” 

	Signature Entertainment’s survival sequel “Fall 2” opened in sixth place with $648,421. “Insidious: Out of the Further,” distributed by Sony, followed in seventh position in its fourth week, adding $619,084 to raise its running total to $9.9 million. 

	Entertainment Film Distributors’ action thriller “Runner,” starring Alan Ritchson and Owen Wilson, bowed in eighth place with $517,727. Paramount landed the ninth spot with the 45th anniversary 4K re-issue of “Raiders of the Lost Ark,” which grossed $326,263. Altitude Film Distribution’s “Coyote vs. Acme” rounded out the top 10 in its fourth frame, collecting $188,463 to push its cume to $2.6 million.
	

	Looking ahead to the upcoming theatrical frame, rollouts begin mid-week with Seventh Art Productions’ “Exhibition On Screen: James McNeill Whistler 2026,” followed Move Over Productions’ documentary “The Route to Cappyness.”

	Wide commercial openings on Friday across 300+ locations are led by “Resident Evil,” distributed by Sony, and Paramount’s “Bad Apples,” starring Saoirse Ronan. 

	Releases also include Screenbound Pictures’ music documentary “50 Years of Punk,” Entertainmeny Film Distributors’ “De Gaulle: Part 2 – Liberté,” Aardman’s “Shaun the Sheep: The Beast of Mossy Bottom,” from Studiocanal, Dogwoof’s “The Cycle of Love,” Curzon’s “Queen at Sea,” Other Parties’ “Barrio Triste,” Sonorous Films’ “Premature,” Shane O’Sullivan’s documentary “The Watergate Caper: Richard Nixon and the Death of the American Dream,” from E2 Films, Mubi’s “Pulp: What Do You Do For An Encore?” and Anime Ltd’s “Whisper of the Heart.” The weekend concludes on Saturday with the event cinema broadcast of “Twenty Years of the Met in Cinemas: An Anniversary Celebration” from Trafalgar Releasing.

schema.headline: ‘Practical Magic 2’ Casts a Spell Over U.K., Ireland Box Office as Oasis Doc Rocks No. 2

title: Barcelona’s Serielizados Pro Reveals Program and Mind the Gap Co-Pro Pitch: Carlos Marques-Marcet, Vilapuig Sisters Make the Cut (EXCLUSIVE)
description: Acclaimed Catalan filmmaker Carlos Marques-Marcet (“10,000 km,” TIFF Platform winner “They Will Be Dust”), with his first showrunning gig, and siste
body:
Acclaimed Catalan filmmaker Carlos Marques-Marcet (“10,000 km,” TIFF Platform winner “They Will Be Dust”), with his first showrunning gig, and sisters Mireia and Joana Vilapuig (“Selftape”) will rub shoulders with creators from Galicia, Finland, Iceland, Latvia, Mexico and Portugal at the second edition of iSerielizados Mind the Gap co-pro series contest.

	The international series pitch, due to unspool Oct 21 in Barcelona, is the pièce de résistance of series festival Serielizados’ fast-expanding industry confab Serielizados Pro, running Oct. 21-24.
	

	On the heels of last year’s flawless launch of Mind the Gap, set up to boost top-tier series in their financial stage of financing, more than double the number of projects from a bigger geographical spread were submitted this year.

	Out of the 11 selected titles, eight came from open calls, and three were invited by European industry partners Seriencamp, ECAM Forum and Iberseries.



	

					Victor Sala
									Credit: Victor Parreno
	



	“It’s been more challenging for our selection committee but also extremely exciting,” said Victor Sala, Serielizados Pro honcho who welcomed new collaborations with the Baltics, through Latvia’s entry “The Man Behind a Mask,” and the sustained ‘love affair’ between Finland and Spain.

	“Apart from Spain – obviously!, we received the largest number of projects from Finland – five or six”, said the industry chief who picked with his team the Finnish ‘crime “Bloodwine” from Helsinki-filmi (“The Summer Book,” “Codename-Annika”) and psycho drama “Dangerous Woman” from Gutsy Pictures (“L/Over”). Sala also underscored Helsinki-based Tekele’s involvement in the Spanish dramedy “Not Girls”, first original series produced by top Catalan banner Fasten Films (“The End of It”).
	

	“We are really happy that renowned Catalan directors and showrunners trust Mind the Gap as a place to find partners,” added Sala, referring to “Callback,” co-penned by the Vilapuig sisters with Diego Vega, and “Act of Faith,” the first TV show created by Goya and Toronto Platform winning helmer Marques-Marcet.

	While “Callback” deals with “the grey areas of abuse where aggression is subtle and it’s difficult to establish clear roles between victim and agressor,” according to Jordina Casals from Funicular Films (“This is Not Sweden”), “Act of Faith” offers a new twist to the political thriller. Indeed, the show centers not on the real cases of undercover cops that infiltrated social movements in Spain, but on the victims, friends and lovers who felt betrayed.

	“Storytellers remind us that the world is not easy to grasp, that reality is more complex than we initially thought,” noted Sala, himself co-writer of Serielizados’ opener “In Vitro (HBO Max-3Cat) which offers a kaleidoscopic – even ironic – look at fertility in the 21st century.

	This year’s international jury which will hand out the €5,500 ($6,300) prize for Mind the Gap best project takes in Mubi’s Ben Driscoll, Movistar Plus’ Susanna Herreras, Beta Film’s Peter Lohner, ZDF Studios’ Susanne Frank and Arte France’s Virginie Béjot. An additional €2,000 ($2,300) Konga Music Agency Award will be bestowed to the best Spanish project.

	Masterclasses with Series Heavyweights

	Other Serielizados Pro highlights take in masterclasses with showrunner Steven Moffat (“Sherlock,” “Doctor Who”) and producer Sue Vertue, “In Treatment” creator Hagai Levi, whose latest show “Etty “will bow in competition at Serielizados, and seasoned Spanish scribes Isabel Peña (“The Beloved,” “The New Years”), and Eduardo Villanueva (“Riot Police,” “La Ruta”).

	Movistar PlusRodrigo Sorogoyen’s regular writing partner Peña and Villanueva will discuss their latest show — the Movistar Plus Original “El Castillo” which will bow in Barcelona on the heels of its world premiere out of competition in San Sebastian.



	

					El Castillo
									Courtesy of Movistar Plus
	



	In another inspiring session sponsored by Seriel Eye, German creator and showrunner Alexander Lindh will discuss a world without prisons, portrayed in his high-end show ”A Better Place,” competing at Serielizados for best international series.
	

	Tracker of market trends and networking facilitator, the boutique Serielizados Pro will also host discussions about the state of European series development, production, distribution, new digital strategies, with key industry players including The Mediapro Studios’ Béatrice Nouh, DR Sales’ Ella Glantz, Oble’s Katia Sol, RTVE Play’s Alberto Fernández and Tallinn TV Beats’ Roosa Toivonen among others.

	Turning the lens on the thriving Catalan audiovisual industry, Serielizados organisers will invite the 300-plus attendees to a session on the state of series production in the region, and a case study on the two successful co-productions “In Vitro,” (3Cat-HBO Max) and “Segunda temporada” (Filmin), the festival’s opening and closing bets.

	To honor the best of the best Spanish series, a new Audiovisual 451 Award will be handed out for its inaugural session to HBO Max’s acquisition and 3Cat’s drama departments for their joint efforts to deliver “some of the most relevant series in recent years, such as “Pubertat,” “Ravalear” and this year’s “In Vitro,” distinguished by their compelling themes and high production values,” said Audiovisual 451 journalist Irene Jiménes. ” In times of fierce industry competition, budget constraints and editorial cancellations, it is admirable that a global platform and a public broadcaster have overcome their differences to make these co-productions a reality,” she added.

	Serielizados Pro is backed by ICEC (Catalan Institute for Cultural Companies), DAMA, Triodos Bank, PROA, Konga Music Agency, Sarao Music, Serial Eyes, and Antaviana and AVisual Pro.

	The 13th edition of the series festival will run Oct.19-28 in Barcelona and on the upscale streamer Filmin Nov. 10-22.

	A Full rundown of Mind the Gap Projects, 2026:

	“Act of Faith,” (“Acte de fe,” 4X45’, Spain)Written, directed by Carlos Marques-MarcetProduced by Suica Films and Abacus

	In his first series as a creator, multi-awarded Catalan auteur Marques-Marcet has taken as starting points real cases of left-wing pro-independence activists who were infiltrated by undercover cops in Spain, to deliver a suspense drama about intimacy, trust and betrayal. “At its heart lies a question we have all asked ourselves: Do I really know the people I love?”, says Suica Films’ Alba Bosch.
	

	“Bloodwine,” (“Veriviini,” 6X45’, Finland, France)Written by Katri Järvelä, Tua HarnoProduced by Helsinki-filmi, Finland for MTV Finland, with France’s CineFrance

	“Bloodwine” is a delicious crime series set in the lush world of French vineyards, exquisite palates, and the unique million-dollar business wine fraud. We want the audience to watch the series and then look at their glass of wine thinking: what’s actually in my glass,” says Helsinki-filmi head of drama Mia Ylönen,

	“Callback,” (4X40’, Spain)Created and written by Joana Vilapuig, Mireia Vilapuig and Diego Vega,Produced by Funicular Films (“This is Not Sweden”) and Left Tackle Films.

	In their second series set in show business after “Selftape,” the Vilapuig sisters focus on Fran, a filmmaker who accuses Román, her actor and producer of abuse, in the middle of the premiere of her directorial debut at a European Film Festival. “At its core, ‘Callback’ explores a relationship marked by an abuse of power and how a personal conflict can become a broader social and political debate,” says Funicular Films’ Jordina Casals.

	“Dangerous Woman,” (6X42’, Finland)Written by Kevin Rundle from an idea by Gutsy Pictures founder Marika MakaroffProduced by Gutsy Pictures

	After the Canneseries 2025 entry “L/over” which turned on coercive control and its dramatic effects, Gutsy Pictures’ new psychological drama looks at a woman’s track record as a violent person. But is she really a villain or a victim?

	“El Observatorio,” (6X45’, Spain)Project selected at ECAM Forum 2026 where it won the Serielizados AwardCreated-written by Laura Roqué, Eloy Zamora and Luis Sorolla

	A drama comedy set in Andalusia, 2011. In a small village of a Sierra Morena threatened by depopulation, sheep graze alongside a colossal astronomical observatory. The only people working there are astrophysicists Sara and Gabi. When a light suddenly appears in the sky, Sara believes the light could be her late father communicating with her. “Our project explores what happens to us when our belief system enters into a crisis,” says Roqué who is seeking a producer and financial partners.

	“Gusgus,” (6X55’, Iceland, Benelux)Project selected at Seriencamp where it scooped the Co-Production Pitch Award.Created and written by Arni & Kinski, Lawrence Inglee
	

	Produced by Truenorth Nordic for RÚV, in co-production with Lumière, BeneluxA semi-autobiographical show about electronic band GusGus. How nine young artists set out to become the biggest band in the world, until one member’s private tragedy fractures their ascent. “Against our lead characters deeply personal journey through grief is the extraordinary world of Iceland in the 1990s: a small, isolated island where musicians, filmmakers and artists seem to be inventing a new reality,” says band co-founder Stefan Arni.

	“Historia de Espías, The Obedient Assassin,” (6X60’, Mexico, Spain)Project selected at IberseriesCreated and written by Salvador Rizo, with co-writer Alessandro PederzoliDirected by Horacio Alcalà

	Produced by The Maestros, Mexico, with The Aurora Project, a Spanishanthology TV show based on the spy book series by John P. Davidson. In Season 1, “The Obedient Assassin,” the story turns on the former Soviet Union agency NKVD’ s efforts to assassinate Leon Trotsky in exile in Mexico. “Our ambition is to build a map of real espionage across nationalities and decades, with a different story every time,” says producer Pederzoli.

	“Karbo FC,” (6X45’, Spain)Created by Sonia MéndezProduced by Cósmica Productions, Accidental Films



	

					Karbo FC
									Courtesy of Cósmica Productions
	



	A first TV drama produced by Galicia-based Cósmica, based on an idea by the banner’s co-founder, football fan, writer and director Sonia Mendez (“As Neves”). A feelgood coming of age tale based on true events, about a group of working class girls who defy prejudice in 1980s Spain to live their dream-playing football for the Karbo FC.

	“Line,” (“Linha,” 6X30′, Portugal)Created by Hermano MoreiraProduced by Manilha Filmes (Hotel Amor”) and SPi (“Cold Haven”)

	At an ecstatic dance festival, almost nothing is what it seems. The lines between racism, sexual harassment and drug addiction are very thin and shift depending on the perspective from five different characters.

	“The Man Behind a Mask,” (Latvia)Created by Anna Kalnina, Serge SerpuhovsProduced by Baltic Pine Films, Latvia

	Based on the true story of a Latvian doctor, a medical pioneer, innovator and rule-breaker whose career intersected medicine, politics and power. “At its core, ‘The Man Behind a Mask’ is about a healer forced to become an instrument of the state, a man torn between his calling to heal and his duty to serve the system,” says Serpuhovs, executive producer at Riga-based production and servicing outfit Baltic Pine Films.
	

	“Not Girls,” (“Noies no,” Spain, Finland)Written by Indigo Carbajal, Jana Jubert, Tomàs BayoDirected by Celia GiraldoProduced by Fasten Films, Spain for 3Cat, in co-production with Tekele, Finland

	The first original series from top Spanish banner Fasten Films present at Cannes this year with “The End of It,” “Strawberries,” “Rehearsals for a Revolution.” A bold contemporary dramedy set in Barcelona’s vibrant music and cultural scene in which members of a pop-rock band learn to deal with ambition, jealousy, desire and belonging.

schema.headline: Barcelona’s Serielizados Pro Reveals Program and Mind the Gap Co-Pro Pitch: Carlos Marques-Marcet, Vilapuig Sisters Make the Cut (EXCLUSIVE)

title: San Sebastian and Busan Title ‘In My Father’s Room’ Sells Wide for Bitters End (EXCLUSIVE)
description: Bitters End has sold “In My Father’s Room” to France, Korea, Taiwan and Hong Kong ahead of the film’s world premiere in competition at the San Sebas
body:
Bitters End has sold “In My Father’s Room” to France, Korea, Taiwan and Hong Kong ahead of the film’s world premiere in competition at the San Sebastian Film Festival, with several more territories still in negotiation. 

	After San Sebastian, the film will travel to the Busan International Film Festival.

	Art House Films has picked up France, Jinjin Pictures takes Korea, Sky Digi Entertainment has Taiwan and Edko Films holds Hong Kong.
	

	“A truly beautiful film. I was struck by the compositions, the contrasts, and the precision of the framing. What I loved most was its remarkable ability to move naturally between different art forms and weave them into everyday life. Deeply moving in its belief that art is what gives meaning to life,” said Eric Le Bot, president of Art House Films.


	“In My Father’s Room,” known in Japan as “Muyou no Hito,” marks the feature directorial debut of best-selling novelist Maha Harada, adapted from her own short story “An Unnecessary Man.” The cast includes Aoi Yu (“Wife of a Spy”), Ogata Issey (“Onoda,” “Silence,” “Yi Yi”), Nagayama Eita (“Monster”) and Watanabe Eri (“Shall We Dance?”), with Kitagawa Yoshio, whose credits include “Evil Doesn’t Exist” and “Lost Land,” serving as cinematographer.

	The story follows Satomi, an employee at an art museum, after an envelope arrives bearing an unfamiliar key. It unlocks a room left behind by her father, dead a month earlier and alone at the time. Tracing what he did in his last days, Satomi uncovers a figure society had largely written off, one who nonetheless took quiet comfort in language, in tea ceremony and in small, overlooked beauty, and she comes to recognize the grace in how he lived.
	

	Bitters End will also handle the film’s local release, scheduled for January 2027 in Japan.

title: Mariska Hargitay Leads a Brisk Yet Celebratory Emmys in a Return to Form: TV Review
description: Last year, the Emmys bet on an unorthodox host in Nate Bargatze and the result was an unmitigated disaster. This year, the Emmys bet on an unorthodo
body:
Last year, the Emmys bet on an unorthodox host in Nate Bargatze and the result was an unmitigated disaster. This year, the Emmys bet on an unorthodox host and were rewarded with an effusive, yet efficient tribute to television at its best.

	Watching “Law & Order: Special Victims Unit” star — and “My Mom Jayne” director, and Broadway leading lady and New York Knicks superfan — Mariska Hargitay emcee the Emmy awards’ 78th ceremony, I thought often of stand-up comedian Nikki Glaser. After Jo Koy’s abysmal, contemptuous turn leading the Golden Globes, Glaser rescued the broadcast, raised her own profile and ultimately became a repeat host by embracing enthusiasm. And while Bargatze’s Emmys performance last year wasn’t quite as infamous as Koy’s, a countdown clock preemptively chiding honorees for enjoying their moment a little too much showed a similar lack of regard for the evening’s ostensible purpose. Hargitay went in the other direction, throwing herself into multiple musical numbers and generally showing herself to be a fan of television as well as one of its most visible ambassadors. The approach paid off.
	

	It helped that Hargitay, while game, wasn’t exactly earnest: a seemingly sincere monologue about the power of storytelling turned out to be a feint, transitioning into a ripoff of the AMC Nicole Kidman ad called out by the Australian actor herself. (The bit was also a self-aware wink on the part of Kidman, who Hargitay brushed off as “movie lady” but spends most of her time on the small screen these days.) But the novice host clearly took the job seriously, going through more outfit changes than her good friend Taylor Swift on an average night of the Eras Tour. Hargitay even got Swift herself to show up for a pre-taped segment, even if the cameo didn’t entirely justify an overlong parody of the pop star’s conspiratorial fanbase.
	

	The Emmys had room to spare because the show had bumped several awards to the earlier ceremony once known as the Creative Arts Emmys, including supporting actor and actress in a limited series. (Winners Linda Cardellini and David Harbour of “DTF St. Louis” still got to appear in the main show as presenters.) The move was controversial — when the Oscars tried something similar a few years ago, demoting most of the technical awards to a pre-show, the time savings weren’t enough to justify the slight and the strategy was swiftly reversed.

	But on Sunday at the Emmys, the results spoke for themselves with a brisk show that miraculously came in a few minutes under time. One Hargitay-led song, a riff on Supertramp’s “Goodbye Stranger” repurposed into an ode to series finales with an assist from Andrew Rannells, wasn’t necessary. But a dedicated tribute to Dolly Parton, led by fellow country luminary Reba McEntire, was certainly nice to have — as were extended honors for Catherine O’Hara and Rob Reiner. Even letting John Mulaney riff for several minutes before presenting lead actor in a drama felt like a good use of airtime. After all, the award itself was almost an afterthought: everyone in the room knew it was about to go to Noah Wyle of “The Pitt” once again, and deservedly so.

	The modern Emmys love a sweep, which can give the proceedings a monotonous feel. It’s nonetheless hard to begrudge the love for horror comedy “Widow’s Bay,” a tide so strong it seemingly transcended categories and propelled star Matthew Rhys to a double acting win for his turn in Netflix’s “The Beast in Me” as well as the Apple TV breakout. An original story and therefore an underdog, “Widow’s Bay” also yielded the best speech of the night in creator Katie Dippold’s commitment to shamelessly show off her new trophy. And the plaudits were more evenly distributed in drama, which delivered surprise wins for Allison Janney of “The Diplomat,” Tom Pelphrey of “Task” and, to my personal delight, director Saul Metzstein of “Slow Horses.”

	An unexpected result is not always the best one; much as I love Sally Field, I’m baffled by her performance in “Remarkably Bright Creatures” edged out Sarah Pidgeon’s bewitching embodiment of Carolyn Bessette in “Love Story.” It’s still good to know the Emmys can veer a bit off book in its production choices and deliver a solid, enjoyable show. After all, the pool of late night luminaries from which networks have reliably drawn their awards talent is shrinking, despite Stephen Colbert’s pleas to preserve the institution as a talent pipeline after the cancellation of “The Late Show.” Figures like Hargitay — familiar mainstays, but with untapped reserves of talent — are now the next best option in the search for steady hands. Hargitay herself, we’ve seen, was more than ready to step up to the plate.

schema.headline: Mariska Hargitay Leads a Brisk Yet Celebratory Emmys in a Return to Form: TV Review

title: Emmys 2026 Snubs and Surprises: Colbert’s Final Season Wins, Oscar Isaac Can’t Stop Matthew Rhys, Taylor Swift Crashes the Party and More
description:
The 78th Primetime Emmy Awards are here, and much like a passing glance at a cloudless night sky, the stars are out!

	But this is no time for puns!
body:
The 78th Primetime Emmy Awards are here, and much like a passing glance at a cloudless night sky, the stars are out!

	But this is no time for puns! Television’s biggest night was hosted by “Law & Order: Special Victims Unit” icon Mariska Hargitay, and there were plenty of big wins and upsets.

	See some of the night’s biggest snubs and surprises below.

	
		Surprise: “DTF St. Louis” takes limited or anthology series.	

	Despite being a more subtle character study compared to buzzy heavy hitters like the second season of “Beef” and the Matthew Rhys-led “The Beast in Me,” it ended up with seven statues, including top honors.
	
	
		Snub: Actors who aren’t white.	

	My colleague Clayton Davis wrote about it at length, but every lead and supporting acting award went to a white performer this year. Why is this still happening in 2026?
	
		Surprise: Taylor Swift was in two places at once.	

	Swift did indeed support her BFF Hargitay’s hosting gig, pre-taping a comedy sketch so she could also attend her husband Travis Kelce’s first game of the season with the Kansas City Chiefs.
	
		Snub: Oscar Isaac can’t block a record evening.	

	Isaac’s performance in “Beef” was predicted to win by the pundits, but Rhys pulled off a record win, taking both lead actor in a limited or anthology series or movie and lead actor in a comedy series.
	
		Surprise: “Slow Horses” takes drama directing honor.	

	With starry and showy noms like Noah Wyle and Vince Gilligan, “Slow Horses” director Saul Metzstein sneaked in with a win for the episode “Scars.”
	
	
		Snub: The supporting actresses of “The Pitt” cancel each other out.	

	While Allison Janney is brilliant, it’s likely that “Pitt” vote splitting opened the lane for her work on “The Diplomat” to be recognized.
	
		Surprise: Gilligan nabs writing honor for “Pluribus.”	

	The writing category is always full of surprises, and the dramatic side of the category was no different, with Gilligan’s out-there “Pluribus” besting more down-to-earth storytelling.
	
		Surprise: Stephen Colbert’s final season of “The Late Show” takes home variety series kudos.	

	A bit of background: In 2015, outstanding variety series was broken into two categories: outstanding variety sketch series and outstanding talk series. This year, the split was reversed; the categories were merged. Given all of the controversy about his show ending, Colbert certainly had a shot at winning the combined category, as he won talk series last year. But it had to squeeze by the juggernaut of John Oliver’s “Last Week Tonight,” which consistently won the variety sketch series statue.
	
		Surprise: John Mulaney delivers a tight stand-up segment an hour into the show.	

	It’s no surprise that Mulaney was funny, but his introduction to lead actor in a dramatic series squeezed so many laughs and inside-baseball showbiz jokes that it gave the night a great jolt. Also bonus for nominee Mark Ruffalo chuckling along in the crowd. That man deserves a hearty laugh!
	
		Surprise: Kate O’Flynn takes home hardware for the year’s wackiest character.	

	Despite what the pundits may have predicted, it seems so wonderful that a character as deliciously weird as Patricia Moyer can be victorious at a major award show. O’Flynn is just too undeniable on “Widow’s Bay.”
	
		Surprise: The show was three minutes short!	

	Brevity is the soul of wit, and this year’s ceremony kept things tight! “Leave ’em wanting more” is a mantra that other award shows could stand to learn …
	
		Surprise: Palpable sexual tension between Hargitay and Jean Smart in the opening segment!	

	There was a moment that, while the duo was lounging in bed together watching TV, Smart gave an unmistakable look to her bedmate. Should have kept that camera rolling!
	
		Snub: Fashion lovers looking for some entertainment.	

	Very few celebs brought their A-game to the red carpet and ceremony. Let’s spice things up a bit next year!
	
	
		Surprise: Why would the Emmys air opposite Monday Night Football?	

	Believe it or not, there are many TV addicts who also love sports. It’s the first week of the NFL returning, the year’s first Monday Night Football and it’s a Kansas City Chiefs game. Award show ratings are struggling … why go up against a gridiron giant?

schema.headline: Emmys 2026 Snubs and Surprises: Colbert’s Final Season Wins, Oscar Isaac Can’t Stop Matthew Rhys, Taylor Swift Crashes the Party and More

title: Apple TV Wins 28 Emmys Thanks to ‘Widow’s Bay’ Sweep, HBO Max Takes Second Place With Help From ‘The Pitt’ and ‘DTF St. Louis’
description:
“Widow’s Bay” was the most-awarded show at the Emmys this year, winning 14 trophies total.

	The Apple TV comedy already had eight wins under its be
body:
“Widow’s Bay” was the most-awarded show at the Emmys this year, winning 14 trophies total.

	The Apple TV comedy already had eight wins under its belt at the start of Monday night’s ceremony, having picked up awards including guest comedy actress (Betty Gilpin), comedy casting and music supervision at last week’s Creative Arts Emmys. At the Primetime Emmys, it won every category it was nominated for, adding six to its haul: outstanding comedy series, lead comedy actor (Matthew Rhys), supporting comedy actor (Stephen Root), supporting comedy actress (Kate O’Flynn), comedy writing and comedy directing. This was a record-breaking sweep: “Widow’s Bay” has now won more Emmys in a single year than any comedy series in history.
	

	As a result, Apple TV was the most successful studio at the Emmys this year. The tech giant-turned-streamer took home 28 trophies total, including six “Pluribus” wins, three for “Margo’s Got Money Troubles,” three for “Palm Royale,” one for “Slow Horses” and one for “Mr. Scorsese.”


	This is the first time at the top of the tally for Apple, a major achievement indicating continued growth after it had the No. 1 show last year — “The Studio” with a then-record-breaking 13 wins — but still trailed behind HBO Max and Netflix overall. In fact, 2026 marks only the second time in 20 years that a platform besides HBO Max or Netflix has led the Emmys. (FX triumphed over them in 2024.)

	HBO Max came in second place this year with 21 Emmys. At the top of the heap with seven awards each were “DTF St. Louis” and “The Pitt,” which were named outstanding limited series and outstanding drama series, respectively. They tied with two other shows to become the titles with the second-most wins after “Widow’s Bay”: “The Traitors” on Peacock and “The Apple Music Super Bowl LX Halftime Show Starring Bad Bunny” on NBC.
	

	With its six awards for Apple, “Pluribus” tied with “The Late Show With Stephen Colbert” as the third winningest show at the Emmys. Fourth, fifth and sixth place went, respectively, to “Spider-Noir” with five wins, “The Muppet Show” with four and “Beef” with three — with each of the three shows earning all of its gold at the Creative Arts Emmys rather than the primetime ceremony.

	After HBO Max, as the No. 3 platform, was Netflix with 16 wins spread quite evenly across “Beef,” “Love on the Spectrum,” “Bridgerton,” “The Beast in Me” and more.

	See a full breakdown below of the Emmys by program and by platform below.

title: Stephen Colbert Says ‘Free Speech Is Alive and Well’ After Emmy Win Despite CBS Cancellation: Late Night Is ‘Just as Vital as it Ever Has Been’
description: “The Late Show With Stephen Colbert” may have been canceled by CBS, but after taking home the award for outstanding variety series at Monday night’s
body:
“The Late Show With Stephen Colbert” may have been canceled by CBS, but after taking home the award for outstanding variety series at Monday night’s Emmy Awards, Stephen Colbert is still optimistic about the state of late-night television.Speaking with CNN correspondent Elizabeth Wagmeister and Variety co-president and co-editor-in-chief Ramin Setoodeh following the Emmy Awards, Colbert explained that he still feels that “free speech is alive and well.”“Because if you can’t say something because you go to jail, that is a violation of free speech,” he continued. “I think that late night is just as funny and just as vital as it ever has been, and I love watching Jimmy and Jimmy and John and John and Seth and everybody else. And I think I hope it goes on for a long time because you get to work with people like this, and that’s the greatest gift.”“The Late Show With Stephen Colbert” won the award for its final season, which ended in May after CBS announced the series’ cancellation. The show was up for the Emmy against “The Daily Show” (Comedy Central), “Jimmy Kimmel Live!” (ABC), “Last Week Tonight With John Oliver” (HBO Max) and “Saturday Night Live” (NBC).Speaking with Wagmeister and Setoodeh, Colbert also playfully pivoted away from the topic of Donald Trump: “That’s a beautiful dress. It’s amazing. What? Oh, I’m sorry, I’m deaf in that ear,” he said when asked if he thinks his show was canceled by the president. As for his thoughts on Bari Weiss, Colbert said he’s “never heard of her. Do you know her? I hear great things.”



	The host also noted that he feels “just lovely” following the win. “I’m so glad that the show got recognized, and especially last week, all the people who want the creative arts, the writers and our director, our technical director, camera, lighting, and the digital team, and then tonight, all these incredible people,” he said. “First of all, just to be together after not seeing these guys for four months, it’s incredible. And we couldn’t be more grateful to the academy and everybody who voted for the show.”Prior to Monday night’s awards, “The Late Show” had already won four prizes during the first weekend of the Emmys: Outstanding Writing For A Variety Series, Outstanding Directing For A Variety Series, Outstanding Technical Direction and Camerawork For A Series, Outstanding Lighting Design/Lighting Direction For A Series and Outstanding Picture Editing For Variety Programming (Segment).

schema.headline: Stephen Colbert Says ‘Free Speech Is Alive and Well’ After Emmy Win Despite CBS Cancellation: Late Night Is ‘Just as Vital as it Ever Has Been’

title: ‘The Life and Deaths of Wilson Shedd’ Review: Amanda Seyfried and Scoot McNairy Are Powerful in Tim Blake Nelson’s Twisty Dark-Side Prison Saga
description: Tim Blake Nelson’s “The Life and Deaths of Wilson Shedd” is a gripping, wrenching, dark-as-midnight crime drama that taps into a phenomenon many mig
body:
Tim Blake Nelson’s “The Life and Deaths of Wilson Shedd” is a gripping, wrenching, dark-as-midnight crime drama that taps into a phenomenon many might view as an underground secret (or maybe they just don’t know enough about it): the relationship that develops, more often than you’d think, between incarcerated violent criminals and civilians who fall in love with them. Often, it starts with an exchange of letters. But in “The Life and Deaths of Wilson Shedd,” Karen (Amanda Seyfried), a teacher who’s looking for an escape from her oppressive marriage and her dead-end life, finds work leading a creative-writing class at a maximum-security prison in Oklahoma.
	

	One of the prisoners, Wilson Shedd (Scoot McNairy), has a snaky menace about him, but he’s clearly intelligent, and he’s actually interested in reading Hemingway short stories and trying his own hand at writing. When one of the other prisoners starts to bait Karen with hostile leering comments, Wilson warns him to back down. (When he doesn’t, the situation gets taken care of in a bloodier way.) With his quiet drawl and sociopathic flatness, Wilson has a mean charm that sneaks up on you, though it takes the audience a while to realize what he’s up to regarding Karen. He’s playing her.


	Early on, there’s a jarring cut: to a scene of Wilson and two other prisoners in the outside world, still in their dirty orange prison uniforms, using an axe to bust into someone’s home. They have obviously escaped. But this is quite the dramatic flash-forward, and it sets the tone and structure of the movie — that Nelson, who wrote and directed it, is going to be jumping around in chronology, in what feels almost like a “Pulp Fiction” time loop, to undercut any tidy narrative stability. The fractured time scheme works powerfully; it keeps the audience on edge and triggers connections we wouldn’t otherwise make.
	

	That said, to plug into the drama of “The Life and Deaths of Wilson Shedd,” you need to accept that Amanda Seyfried’s Karen, who seems smart and canny and aware of things, could start receiving confessional letters from a prisoner like Wilson and be seduced by them — drawn into his spell of damaged “vulnerability.” Surveying Seyfried’s no-nonsense crispness, you might say, “Nope, that wouldn’t happen.” But the film lays the emotional groundwork for it (she convinces herself that he can save her), and part of what’s scary and fascinating is that what happens does chafe against our common sense, and the common sense we want our heroine to have. This, the film seems to be saying, is not a rational relationship. It’s a bond of counterintuitive danger, and that’s its allure.

	Tim Blake Nelson is a great actor who’s been directing independent dramas for 30 years. I’ve been a fan ever since I saw his first one, “Eye of God” (also a bleak crime film with a tricky time scheme), back at the Sundance Film Festival in 1997. I thought he became major with “The Grey Zone” (2001), a Holocaust drama unlike any other. It put you right there in the camps, along with the Sonderkommando (the Jewish prisoners who led victims into the gas chambers and then disposed of the bodies); it had a queasiness you couldn’t shake off. “The Life and Deaths of Wilson Shedd” is only Nelson’s sixth feature, and it’s his strongest since “The Grey Zone.” It holds you with the stark realism of its craft (this is a film about criminals but not a “thriller”), and with what it’s about: how human violence carves out its own realm of existence, and then feeds on itself.

	The staging has an ominous matter-of-fact authority, whether it’s Karen fighting with her lout of a husband (Grant Harvey) or Wilson using the hardware-store tools Karen sneaks into him to start chiseling away at his escape. I’ve never seen Scoot McNairy give a performance this rich — it’s as if he’s playing someone like Gary Gilmore, his personality wary and contained, magnetically so, until he draws on the violence that’s been simmering in him for a lifetime. (Even when he does, it’s contained.) There’s a nice Black family, the Lawsons (William Jackson Harper and Devyn A. Tyler), who are taking a trip with their kids (Xuri Selah and Eric Blount) in their SUV, and what happens to them on a picnic is so horrifying that I nearly had to turn away. Yet Nelson directs a scene like this with unfussy bravura, so that there’s a need to look, to confront what evil is.
	

	There’s one more level of violence in “The Life and Deaths of Wilson Shedd.” Let’s call it state-sanctioned violence. What should we do with people like Wilson Shedd? Should they become the lightning rod of our vengeance? Or if not, are we refusing to close the circle? There is nothing supernatural about “The Life and Deaths of Wilson Shedd,” but as the film’s title suggests, Wilson undergoes more than one death. There’s the one that society hands him. And there’s the one he inflicted on himself, the one we might call not soul murder but soul suicide. Maybe society should have left it there, but you could also say that it’s our responsibility to put a man like this one out of his misery.

schema.headline: ‘The Life and Deaths of Wilson Shedd’ Review: Amanda Seyfried and Scoot McNairy Are Powerful in Tim Blake Nelson’s Twisty Dark-Side Prison Saga

description:
2027 Super Bowl Halftime Show
                          Justin Bieber, Harry Styles On Wish List
body:
2027 Super Bowl Halftime Show
                          Justin Bieber, Harry Styles On Wish List
                      
                  
                                                                        Published 
                              September 15, 2026
                            12:00 AM PDT
                                                                            
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            The folks who call the shots for the Super Bowl halftime show have two megastars at the top of their list for the 2027 event ... Justin Bieber and Harry Styles.
      
    
            Sources tell us both singers are high on Roc Nation's short list. Jay-Z and his company are partnered with the NFL, and as the league's "live music entertainment strategist," Jay has final say on the halftime performer.
      
    
            We're told Justin and Harry have not been approached about the show yet ... and sources tell us Justin and Harry are both unlikely to take the gig if they are finally approached. 
      
    
            The NFL does NOT pay the Super Bowl halftime show performer ... but the artists usually take the gig for exposure and a boost in streaming revenue and ticket sales, especially when they have new music coming out.
      
    
            Justin was involved in the halftime show for the 2026 FIFA World Cup Final earlier this summer.
      
    
            Super Bowl LXI is scheduled for Feb. 14 at SoFi Stadium in Inglewood, CA ... and while that's five months away, the NFL usually announces the halftime performers in late September, which means it could be coming in a matter of weeks.
      
    
            The last time the Super Bowl was held at SoFi, the halftime show included Snoop Dogg, Dr. Dre, Eminem, 50 Cent, Mary J. Blige and Kendrick Lamar.
      
    
            Stay tuned ...

title: Hayden Panettiere's Drug Dealer's Incriminating Texts Focus of DEA Investigation
description:
Hayden Panettiere
                          Drug Dealer's Incriminating Texts Focus of DEA
body:
Hayden Panettiere
                          Drug Dealer's Incriminating Texts Focus of DEA
                      
                  
                                                                        Published 
                              September 15, 2026
                            1:00 AM PDT
                                                                            
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Hayden Panettiere and her drug dealer engaged in numerous text conversations for years -- right up until the week she died -- and the DEA is now laser-focused on the thread of incriminating evidence ... sources tell TMZ.
      
    
            Sources involved in the investigation with direct knowledge tell us ... Hayden and her dealer were very specific about purchasing black market pills. As one source put it, "There are a slew of messages about drugs." We're told the text messages are now a centerpiece of the investigation.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            TMZ broke the story ... the DEA believes Hayden died after taking an oxy pill laced with fentanyl. Our sources say Hayden took various pills with her on the flight from L.A. to South Carolina, the night before she died. Her boyfriend, Brian Hickerson, gave police a bag of Hayden's meds, which could reveal other pills laced with the deadly drug.
      

            And as we reported, Hayden's West Hollywood neighbors say they saw 3 suspicious people coming to Hayden's unit for years. They would come individually, often with a small bag. They saw Hayden open the door, take the bag and the person would leave.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Neighbors suspected the 3 people -- two women and a man -- were drug dealers. The man showed up with a bag the week Hayden died.
      
    
            As for the text messages, there have been other cases where such messages helped authorities nab the drug dealer -- notably in the Mac Miller case, where the dealer went to prison.
      
    
      
      One fatal pill ended Hayden Panettiere’s life.Now, we’re learning more about the deadly drug—and who authorities are investigating in connection with her death. pic.twitter.com/wr1oF7orC3
              @TMZ
  
    
            The toxicology results in Hayden's case will not be available for at least a few weeks.
